planting.note: Divide or transplant established clumps in spring once new shoots emerge; set in humus-rich, evenly moist soil and allow a full season for the slow-spreading rhizomes to establish before expecting a dense mound.

directions: A sport of 'Aureola', this Japanese forest grass carries bright lemon-yellow blades brushed with ivory and chartreuse along arching, cascading stems. Grow in part to full shade with consistently moist, well-drained, organic soil; the gold coloring is brightest in bright shade but scorches in hot afternoon sun. The clump-forming habit spreads gradually by short rhizomes, making it useful as a textural accent in woodland borders, shaded containers, or along shaded path edges. Cut back old foliage in late winter before new shoots emerge.
sources: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Transplant divisions in spring into humus-rich, evenly moist soil in a shaded bed or container; give the arching clump room to spread gently outward over several seasons.

directions: Arising as a shoot mutation of 'Aureola', this forest grass shows creamy green and zesty lime variegated blades on distinctive magenta-tinted stems, forming a graceful cascading mound. Best color and habit develop in part to full shade with cool, humus-rich, consistently moist soil; it struggles in hot, dry sites or intense afternoon sun. Clumps spread slowly and gently, making it a good choice for mass planting as a textured shade groundcover or for softening the edge of a container planting. Remove tattered foliage in late winter ahead of spring regrowth.

planting.note: Set divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained soil enriched with organic matter; established clumps tolerate dry shade once rooted in but flower and clump more densely with regular moisture.

directions: A free-flowering lilyturf selected for its unusually heavy production of dense, upright spikes of rich blue-purple flowers held well above the clumping, dark green grass-like foliage from late summer into autumn. Grows well in partial shade to full sun in ordinary, well-drained garden soil, and the evergreen foliage provides four-season structure in milder climates. Use as edging along shaded paths, as a mass planting under high-canopy trees, or combined with ferns and hostas for textural contrast. Division of congested clumps is best done in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in moist, well-drained soil; the cascading habit shows best when given room to arch outward, such as at a bed edge, slope, or container rim.

directions: This patented evergreen sedge forms a mounded, cascading fountain of narrow, glossy deep-green leaf blades that twist and curl at the tips like falling ribbons. Adaptable to sun or shade, it colors and performs best with afternoon shade and consistently moist, well-drained soil, and tolerates brief dry spells once established. The pendulous habit suits raised beds, slopes, and container edges where the curling foliage can spill over, and it pairs well with bold-leaved hostas or ferns in a woodland setting. Deer and rabbits generally leave it alone.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container starts after soil has warmed in spring; this compact tetraploid sport of 'Sparkler' is slower growing and benefits from average to consistently moist soil in a sheltered, shaded spot.

directions: A dwarf, tetraploid sport of the taller 'Sparkler', this evergreen sedge produces tight whorls of narrow, white-and-green variegated leaf blades radiating outward in a miniature palm-like rosette. Thrives in part sun to light shade in average to moist soil, and its compact scale makes it well suited to woodland garden edges, container accents, or mass drifts where the larger-growing 'Sparkler' would be out of scale. Hardy only where winters stay mild; in colder zones grow it as a container specimen that can be overwintered under cover.

planting.note: Divide established clumps or plant nursery starts in spring or fall in humus-rich soil; this vigorous selection tolerates dense dry shade once established beneath trees.

directions: A robust, densely tufted selection of greater woodrush with broad, glossy, bright green evergreen leaves that take on a yellowed tone through winter. Airy sprays of small brown flowers rise above the foliage in late spring. Exceptionally tolerant of deep, dry shade once rooted in, it makes a tough, impenetrable groundcover beneath mature trees and shrubs where little else will thrive, and its broad leaf texture contrasts well with ferns and finer sedges. Spreads slowly by rhizome and self-sown seedlings, and old foliage can be combed out or sheared in late winter to tidy clumps.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in average, well-drained soil; foliage color is brightest where some direct or filtered sun reaches the clump.

directions: A compact, densely tufted woodrush with glossy, golden-yellow to yellow-green evergreen leaves that intensify in color through late winter and early spring. Airy, bronze-brown flower panicles arch above the foliage from mid-spring into early summer. Unlike many shade-loving Luzula, this selection colors best with some sun to bright shade, making it a good edging or front-of-border plant where it can pick up morning or filtered light. Tolerates average garden soil and occasional dryness once established, and combines well with dark-leaved hostas or heucheras for contrast.

planting.note: Plant divisions on roughly one-foot centers in spring in moist, well-drained soil; being a sterile clumping selection it enlarges gradually rather than spreading aggressively, so space plants closer than typical running ajugas for faster coverage.

directions: An oversized, sterile selection related to the popular 'Black Scallop', with notably larger, glossy, dark purple-black scalloped leaves held in a tight evergreen rosette. Because it does not set seed and spreads only by slowly enlarging clumps and short stolons, it forms a dense, weed-suppressing mat without becoming invasive in beds. Short spikes of blue flowers appear in mid-spring. Grow in part sun to light shade in moist but well-drained soil; it is a good choice for a refined edging plant or small-scale groundcover where running ajugas would be unwelcome.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in moist, well-drained soil; this hybrid selection resists sun scorch better than many ajugas but still colors best with some afternoon shade in hot climates.

directions: A hybrid of Ajuga reptans and Ajuga tenorii bred for small, glossy leaves that emerge flushed with gold, orange, and bronze tones before settling to a mixed warm-colored mat. Low, ground-hugging rosettes spread steadily to form a dense, weed-smothering carpet, with short spikes of blue flowers in spring. Performs well in part sun to light shade in average, well-drained soil, and the bright multicolor foliage is especially effective planted in drifts along path edges or beneath small shrubs where its low height won't be overwhelmed.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in moist, well-drained soil; vigorous stolons fill in quickly, so allow room for the mat to knit together within a season or two.

directions: Another Ajuga reptans x tenorii hybrid from the same breeding program as 'Fancy Finch', this vigorous selection opens with light copper new growth that matures to a soft yellow-tan with contrasting copper veins, turning bronze through winter. Cobalt-blue flower spikes appear in late spring above the low, mat-forming foliage. High resistance to sun scorch lets it hold color better than many gold-leaved ajugas in part sun, though it also performs well in light to medium shade. Useful as a fast-filling, colorful groundcover beneath shrubs or along shaded borders.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in moist, well-drained soil; this selection tolerates more sun than typical ajugas but still appreciates afternoon shade in hot-summer regions.

directions: A pure Ajuga reptans selection bred from a gold-leaved parent crossed with 'Black Scallop', notable for vivid gold foliage marked with bright pink central veins and pink young stolons. Purple-tipped flower stalks carry the typical blue ajuga blooms in spring. Bred for high resistance to sun scorch, it holds its gold color and stays compact even in full sun through summer in cooler climates, while also thriving in part shade elsewhere. Forms a low, dense, colorful mat suited to edging, rock gardens, or mixed groundcover plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in average, well-drained soil; this miniature selection stays restrained and is well suited to combination containers as well as garden beds.

directions: A compact sport of 'Shell Pink' with small, nearly all-silver leaves narrowly edged in green, forming a low, spreading mat topped with light pink flowers from mid-spring into early summer and often again in fall. Its restrained scale makes it a favorite 'spiller' for combination containers, where it won't overrun neighboring plants the way larger lamiums can. In the garden it works well as a weed-smothering groundcover or a mask for fading spring bulb foliage. Grows best in average, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in part to full shade, and resents soggy winter soil and prolonged summer heat and humidity.
